blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Work out total, fixed, variable and average costs from figures, and explain how a change in output moves the averages.

blocks.heading: The working formulas
blocks.text: Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Average total cost = total cost / output; average fixed cost = fixed cost / output; average variable cost = variable cost / output. Otjiwa Dairy in Gobabis pays N$6 000 a month in fixed costs and N$4 for the ingredients of each litre it processes. At 3 000 litres a month its variable costs come to N$4 x 3 000 = N$12 000, so total cost = N$6 000 + N$12 000 = N$18 000.

blocks.heading: The averages, worked through
blocks.text: At those 3 000 litres, average fixed cost = N$6 000 / 3 000 litres = N$2.00 per litre, average variable cost = N$12 000 / 3 000 = N$4.00 per litre, and average total cost = N$18 000 / 3 000 = N$6.00 per litre. At 6 000 litres, variable costs reach N$4 x 6 000 = N$24 000, so total cost = N$6 000 + N$24 000 = N$30 000 and average total cost = N$30 000 / 6 000 = N$5.00 per litre: average fixed cost has fallen to N$1.00 while average variable cost held at N$4.00. A juice bottler in Vietnam runs the same arithmetic on its own figures.

blocks.heading: Why output moves the averages
blocks.text: Average fixed cost falls as output rises because the same fixed payment is spread over more units, and this tends to pull average total cost down at first. Average variable cost is steadier: where each extra litre costs the dairy N$4 in ingredients, the average holds at N$4.00. Where output strains capacity - overtime pay, machine breakdowns, a crowded cold room - the cost of one more unit rises, and average variable cost and average total cost turn upward with it.

blocks.heading: The total cost lines, drawn in words
blocks.text: The dairy's costs can be drawn. Put costs in N$ on the vertical axis and output in litres a month on the horizontal axis. Fixed cost is a horizontal line at N$6 000: the dairy pays the same at zero output as at 6 000 litres. Variable cost starts at the origin, because no output means no ingredients, and rises in a straight line, reaching N$12 000 at 3 000 litres and N$24 000 at 6 000 litres. Total cost starts on the vertical axis at N$6 000 - at zero output the dairy still pays its fixed cost - and rises alongside variable cost, N$6 000 above it at every output: N$18 000 at 3 000 litres and N$30 000 at 6 000 litres. In words, the diagram shows that as output rises, total cost rises only because variable cost rises, and the vertical gap between the total cost and variable cost lines is the fixed cost. Where extra output strains capacity and each litre starts to cost more, the variable cost line steepens, and total cost steepens with it.

blocks.heading: The average cost curves, drawn in words
blocks.text: Average costs go on a separate diagram: cost per unit in N$ on the vertical axis and output on the horizontal axis. Average fixed cost slopes down and flattens out - for the dairy, N$2.00 a litre at 3 000 litres and N$1.00 at 6 000 - because the same N$6 000 is spread over more litres, though it does not reach zero. Average variable cost is usually drawn falling at first, as workers specialise and equipment is used more fully, then flattening, and rising once output strains capacity. Average total cost is average fixed cost plus average variable cost, so it lies above average variable cost by the amount of average fixed cost, and that gap narrows as output rises. Average total cost falls at first, pulled down by falling average fixed cost, and turns upward once rising average variable cost outweighs the fall in average fixed cost, giving a U shape. The diagram shows that the firm's lowest cost per unit sits at the bottom of the average total cost curve; beyond that output, each unit costs more to make.

blocks.text: The revenue set against these costs is section 3.7.3; the objectives that shape how a firm answers a cost rise are section 3.7.5; and the market the firm sells in is topic 3.8.
